Most of the Native Americans were engaged in settled agriculture. Europe and China each had around 60 million people at that time. Within a few decades, the population of the Americas had dropped to just around 5 million people, with over 90% of people perishing due to a combination of infectious diseases and warfare. This population collapse resulted in agriculture being abandoned on a massive scale, resulting in farmland turning wild again. The disruption was big enough that it reduced the amount of CO2 in earth’s atmosphere. Evidence in ice cores from Antarctica shows lower amounts of atmospheric carbon dioxide in samples that are dated to the late 16th century. This reduction in CO2 led to climate change, and scientists now think it may be a key contributor to the phenomenon called the Little Ice Age. The Little Ice Age was a centuries-long period of lower temperatures that affected the North Atlantic region with particular severity. The Little Ice Age eventually ended only when humanity entered its first Industrial Revolution. At its height, the Little Ice Age caused what historians call The General Crisis of the 17th Century in Europe, a period of inclement weather, crop failure, economic hardship, extreme intergroup violence, and high mortality. The General Crisis culminated in the Thirty Years War, a continental-scale war lasting several decades, ending in the year 1648 with the Peace of Westphalia that established the concept of modern nation-states. By the time the Peace of Westphalia was concluded, populations in many regions of Europe had fallen by 70% compared to a generation earlier. ‎<This message was edited>

Basically the answer probability. The regex analysis first identifies a question and possible answer based on whether explicit confirmations are available. Where there are no explicit answer confirmations, claude infers the answer from the chat context.. higher probability means an explicitly confirmed answer exists and that the LLM was able to confirm it independently..
Honestly we only need AI to confirm for about ~30% cases
In general a purely non semantic analysis catches most questions and answers

You can see that for questions where this zero feedback, it has lower confidence and can even mark incorrect answers.  Some kind of confirmation is thus preferable (need not be explicit, even implicit like awarding points) helps
In some cases there is zero response (the chat doesnt export reactions) so it’s hard to detect the answer

As you all know, I am obsessed with history. But this poem by Srirangam Srinivasa Rao aka Sri Sri(Telugu poet from the 20th century) always reminds me what to focus on when trying to understand history. Here is the full poem in translation, thanks to Claude:
*Histories of Nations (Desha Charithralu) — Sri Sri*
I.
Look at the history of any nation, any land —
what is there in it worthy of pride?
The whole tale of the human race, from the start,
is nothing but a creed: oppress, and be satisfied.
II.
The whole tale of the human race, from the start,
is one long war of each against all —
soaked through and through in rivers of battle-blood,
the story of man is the story of the fall.
III.
Grotesque in its themes, demonic in its shape,
cast in the mould of the beast, not the divine —
the whole tale of the human race, from the start,
is the strong feasting on the poor like swine.
IV.
The powerful enslaved the weaker peoples,
chained them, broke them, made them bow the knee —
and those butchers of men became celebrated kings,
their names carved into history with glee.
V.
Search every inch of this earth for a place
that was never once turned into a battlefield —
you will not find it. What the past has left us
is blood, and where there is no blood — tears uncongealed.
VI.
Shattered homes, the grief of countless dying,
the helpless screaming into an empty air —
all of it sinks, unheard, into the pages of history,
buried beneath the weight of those who didn't care.
VII.
Inequality. Greed. Cunning.
Jealousy, rivalry, and deceit —
dressed in the costume of progress and civilization,
this is what history calls a human feat.
VIII.
Genghis Khan — so what? Tamerlane — and then?
Nadir Shah, Ghazni, Ghori — what do the names say?
Alexander the Great — great at what, exactly?
A name is just a name at the end of the day.
IX.
When one force crushed another into dust
and the fallen became the ladder for the strong —
that is where history was born: in the grinding
of power against the powerless, all along.
X.
The long-running deception — still running.
The tyranny of the mighty — still alive.
The coiling venom of the moneyed class —
hasn't it gone far enough? Hasn't it?
XI.
One man crushing another man.
One nation grinding another into the earth.
Is this the sacred social order, then?
Has it not gone on long enough for what it's worth?
XII.
The rickshaw puller on the streets of China,
the mine-worker gasping in Czechoslovakia,
the exhausted oarsman rowing on Ireland's rivers —
all of them cry the same cry, the same failure.
XIII.
The Hottentots, the Zulus, the peoples of Africa —
scattered tribes across whole continents —
choking, straining to speak the raw truth of history
in one voice that rises above the eloquents.
XIV.
Why did this war happen? How long did that empire last?
Dates, documents, proclamations, edicts — no.
These are not the heart of history.
These are the costume. Not the show.
XV.
This queen's romance. That king's petty expenses.
Official explanations. Royal footnotes. No.
These are not the heart of history either.
These are the curtain. Not what lies below.
XVI.
In the dark, unlit corner of the historical record —
barely visible, almost erased from sight —
lie all the stories that were buried on purpose.
Dig them out: truth refuses to stay out of light.
XVII.
Along the Nile, along the great rivers of civilization —
what, exactly, was the life of the ordinary man?
XVIII.
Who ever asks about the laborers
who broke their backs hauling stone upon stone,
to raise the Taj Mahal from the dust of the earth
so an emperor could mourn in marble alone?
XIX.
In the grand military processions of empire,
what courage was it that the common man gave?
The lord rode high in a gilded palanquin —
but who asks about the shoulders that bore his weight?
XX.
Takshashila, Pataliputra —
the ancient shores of the Mediterranean Sea —
Harappa, Mohenjo-daro —
the mouths of the Cro-Magnon caves —
XXI.
Through history's many twilights and dawns,
how did the human story truly grow?
In which land, and in which age,
was the highest purpose actually brought to show?
XXII.
Which sculpture? Which literature? Which science?
Which music rising to the heavens above?
The march toward which luminous dawn?
Which dream? Which conquest? Which undying love?

In the early 2000s, India perfected a "Ghost Protocol"—a method of data transmission that relied entirely on the intentional absence of a completed transaction.
Born from a need to bypass "toll-gate" tariffs, this became a sophisticated social morse code. A single pulse might mean "I’ve arrived," while a double pulse signified "Pick me up." It was a way to transfer information across a network without the network ever realizing a service had been rendered.
Recognizing this "Pulse" as a universal language for the unconnected, many startups transformed it into a massive business engine. By providing consumers with a way to "ping" a brand at zero cost, companies bypassed literacy and financial barriers. The most famous application, Hindustan Unilever’s Kan Khajura Tesan, used this method to build a "radio station" for rural areas, eventually reaching over 100 million people by essentially turning an incomplete signal into a "request for content." and many political parties used this as well for their campaigns. this was killed in 2016 when a giant launches it own brand.
